questions.text: When the user asks to create a token, how does the user prove who they are to the Server? Is that a different login from the API token itself?
What exactly is stored in the api_tokens table for each token (columns), and what does 'Hashed' mean here: which hash, and what is the token string the user sees made of?
questions.about: Tokens go in a new api_tokens table in Postgres. Hashed.

questions.text: How does the Server find the right row when the Client sends a token, if only a hash is stored? What does 'check token' verify (match, expiry, revoked, owner)?
What happens when a Client sends a token that is wrong, expired or revoked? Which 4xx code and what message does it get?
What happens when the user tries to create an 11th token? Does it fail, or replace the oldest? Is the limit counted per user, and do expired or revoked tokens count?
What happens at day 90: is the token deleted, marked, or just rejected at check time? Can the user renew it, or must they create a new one?
What does 'list tokens' return, given the secret is shown once? And what does 'revoke' do to the row (delete or flag), and does it take effect immediately?
Is 'update last used' done before the response, and what happens to the API call if that update fails or is slow? What is last used for?

answers.text: The user is already signed in through the existing session cookie, and create, list and revoke use that cookie through the settings endpoints. The API token is not a login for the settings page. It is used only to call the REST API. The document now says this in Terms.

Columns: id, user_id, name, token_hash (unique), created_at, expires_at, last_used_at (empty means Never), revoked_at (empty means not revoked). token_hash is a SHA-256 of the full token string. The token string is pat_ plus 32 characters from a CSPRNG, and the user sees the whole string once. Reason: a check needs only the fingerprint, and a token with 32 random characters does not need a salt to resist guessing.

The Server hashes the presented token with SHA-256 and looks up that hash through its unique index. It then checks that a row exists, that revoked_at is empty and that expires_at is in the future. The row's user_id is the owner, and the request runs as that user. The owner check applies only to list and revoke.

Missing, unknown, revoked and expired tokens all get HTTP 401 with one identical generic body. If the database check itself fails, the response is 503 and the token is not accepted. Reason: a token that could not be checked cannot be called invalid, and it must not be accepted.

An 11th create is refused with a 4xx and a message that says to revoke a token first. Nothing is replaced. The limit is counted per user over active tokens only, so revoked and expired tokens do not count. A token whose create response was lost still counts until it is revoked or expires.

Nothing deletes the row at day 90. The check rejects it because expires_at has passed, and the list drops it because the list shows active tokens only. It cannot be renewed, so the user creates a new token. The brief states the no-renewal rule.

List returns id, name, created date, expiry date and last used (Never if empty). It never returns the secret. Revoke sets revoked_at and keeps the row. Reason: the row is kept for the record, and the check reads revoked_at on every call. The effect is immediate, because the next API call reads the row and no validity is cached.

last_used_at is written only when it is empty or more than an hour old. The write runs after the response is sent, in the background. If it fails or is slow, the API call still succeeds and the failure is logged without the token. Reason: the brief allows an hour of staleness and forbids a write on every request, and this order means a slow database never delays an API call. last_used is shown on the list so the user can spot unused or stray tokens.

questions.text: In Flow 3, how does the API request get from the Client to the Server, and what is the "Client" here? Does the Server treat it as the same REST API the settings page uses, or a separate one?
questions.about: Flow 3: Client->>Server: API request with Authorization Bearer token

questions.text: Two requests create a token with the same name at nearly the same time, or two creates happen when the user has 9 active tokens. What stops both from succeeding?
questions.about: Flow 1: alt name invalid, or used by one of this user's active tokens / within limit

questions.text: What counts as an invalid name beyond length 1 to 40 (spaces, symbols, case)? And can a name be reused after the old token is revoked or expired?
What do the 4xx and 503 responses look like to the client: is there a body, and does the 503 tell the caller to retry? What does a CI script do when it gets 503 versus 401?
When a request is valid, how does the Server know which user it is acting as, and do tokens have any limits on what they can do (scopes, read vs write), or do they have full access as that user?
Who sees the 'Full token shown once with a Copy button': is the settings page a browser app calling these endpoints, and what does it show when the user closes the dialog or the list refreshes?
questions.about: Create: Full token, shown once with a Copy button

questions.text: What happens if the signed-in session cookie is missing or expired when the user calls create, list or revoke?

answers.text: The Client is any API caller, such as a user's script or CI job, outside the browser. It sends HTTP requests to the same single web/API server that the settings page uses. Tokens are accepted on REST API endpoints. The settings endpoints accept only the session cookie, because the token is for the API and not the settings page. The Terms now define API client and say this.

The create runs under a lock on the user's row, so two creates for the same user run one after the other. Each then sees the other's row for the limit and the name check. The lock lasts only for one create. Without this, both requests could pass both checks. The diagram and notes now show this.

Name reuse: yes, once the old token is revoked or expired, since only active tokens count for uniqueness. Symbols and case: the brief sets only the 1 to 40 length and uniqueness among active tokens, so the plan does not decide which characters are valid or whether case matters. This is listed under Open questions.

4xx responses carry a body with the reason, such as the name message or the limit message. The 401 body is generic and identical in every case. The 503 body is generic and says to retry later. A CI script should retry a 503 after a wait, and treat a 401 as final, since the token is dead and needs replacing. This is now in the failure table and the notes.

A valid token resolves to its row's user_id, so the request runs as that user. The brief sets no scopes or read-only tokens, so the token has the same full access as its user. This is listed as an open question, because it is a security choice the brief did not make.

The settings page is a browser app that calls the create, list and revoke endpoints with the session cookie. The full token appears only in the create response in the open dialog, with a Copy button. The page keeps no copy. Closing the dialog or refreshing the list shows name, dates and last used only, and nobody can show the token again.

A missing or expired session cookie makes create, list and revoke refused the same way the settings endpoints already refuse a signed-out request. The exact existing status and redirect were not checked in the code, and this plan does not change them. An API token is not accepted on these endpoints.

questions.text: In Flow 3, how does the Server tell a token request from a session-cookie request, and what happens if a request carries both a cookie and a Bearer header, or a Bearer header on a settings endpoint?
questions.about: Flow 3: Client->>Server: API request with Authorization Bearer token

questions.text: What is the exact shape of the Bearer header check before hashing: what happens if the header is missing, malformed, or the token does not start with pat_? Does that still reach the database?

What does the user's row lock in Flow 1 lock (which table, which kind of lock), and what happens to a second create that arrives while the first holds it: wait, or fail? What if the lock wait is slow?
questions.about: Server->>DB: Lock this user's row, count active tokens, check the name

questions.text: If two Flow 3 calls arrive close together and both see last_used_at old, do both write it? What does the background write actually run as, and what if the server restarts before it runs?
questions.about: opt last used is empty or over 1 hour old

questions.text: If the create insert hits the unique token_hash (a duplicate generated token), or the DB error comes after the insert succeeded, what does the user see and what is the state?

answers.text: Routes are split by which credential they read. API routes read only the Bearer header, and the settings endpoints read only the session cookie and ignore any Authorization header. This keeps the brief's rule that settings endpoints accept only the cookie. If an API route request carries both, the Bearer token decides the user and the cookie is ignored. Reason: the API caller is a script, and one credential per request keeps the user identity unambiguous. The codebase was not checked for how routes are currently wired, so the split is a plan rule, not a verified fact. The plan now states it in Notes on the flow.

The header is checked before any hash or database read. A missing header, a scheme other than Bearer, an empty token, or a token without the pat_ prefix gets the same 401 body as every other failed check. Reason: no issued token has that form, so the database could not find it, and a cheap local check keeps junk requests off the database. A header that is well formed but has an unknown token still goes to the database lookup, as before. The plan now shows this check in Flow 3.

The lock is a row lock on the user's existing account row, taken in the same transaction as the count and the name check, and held until commit. A second create for the same user waits and does not fail. The wait is short, because the first create only counts rows and inserts one. The plan does not add a lock timeout, since the brief sets none; if the database is down, the create fails like any other database error. The exact table name was not checked in the code, so the plan says account row without naming the table.

Two Flow 3 calls that both see an old last_used_at can both send the write, but the write is one conditional update that changes the row only if it is still empty or over an hour old. The second write then matches no row, so the database does the deduplication. The background write runs on the server's own database connection, not as the user, so it does not carry the user's identity. If the server restarts before the write runs, that write is lost and nothing retries it. Reason: the brief allows an hour of staleness, so the next call after restart writes the value. Last used is best effort by design.

A duplicate token_hash makes the insert fail on the unique index. The transaction rolls back, nothing is saved, and the server returns an error without a token. The user clicks Create again and gets a new token. A clash is not expected with 32 random characters. If the database error comes after the insert but before commit, the commit did not happen, so nothing is saved. If the commit succeeded but its reply was lost, the server returns an error and the row exists with nobody holding the token. That case is the existing lost create response case, so it counts toward the limit until revoked or expired. The token is returned only after commit succeeds, which the plan now states.

teachbacks.text:
1. Starting point. A signed-in user is on Account Settings. The browser holds a session cookie, which is the only credential the create, list and revoke endpoints accept. Everything runs on one web and API server backed by Postgres. A new `api_tokens` table holds one row per token.

2. Create, the request. The user types a name and submits. The browser sends it to the server with the session cookie. If the cookie is missing or expired, the request is refused the way the settings endpoints already refuse signed-out requests. The document does not say what that looks like.

3. Create, the checks. The server opens a database transaction and takes a row lock on the user's existing account row. In the same transaction it counts the user's active tokens and checks the name. Active means not revoked and not past expiry. The name must be 1 to 40 characters and unique among that user's active tokens. The lock stays until commit. A second create from the same user therefore waits for the first, so two creates cannot both slip under the limit.

4. Create, refusals. If the name is invalid or already used by an active token, the server returns a 4xx error with the reason. If the user already has 10 active tokens, it returns a 4xx telling them to revoke one first. Nothing is saved and nothing is replaced in either case.

5. Create, making the token. If the checks pass, the server builds `pat_` plus 32 characters from a CSPRNG. It computes the SHA-256 hash of the token. It inserts a row with `user_id`, `name`, `token_hash`, `created_at` and `expires_at` (created plus 90 days). `last_used_at` and `revoked_at` start empty. Then it commits.

6. Create, the response. Only after the commit succeeds does the server return the full token. The browser shows it once in a dialog with a Copy button. The user copies it into their script or CI secret. The server keeps only the hash. The page keeps no copy, and the token is never in logs or analytics. If the dialog is closed, nobody can show the token again.

7. Create, failures. If the insert fails, the unique `token_hash` clashes, or any error comes before commit, the transaction rolls back and an error is returned. No token is shown, and the user clicks Create again. If the commit succeeds but the response is lost, the row stays and counts toward the limit. The user sees it in the list and can revoke it.

8. List. The user opens the page, or the list refreshes. The server selects that user's active tokens and returns name, created date, expiry date and last used. It never returns the token. Last used shows "Never" where the field is empty. It can be up to an hour stale. Revoked and expired tokens are not listed. An expired row is not deleted. It is just filtered out. If the database read fails, the page shows an error and no partial list.

9. API call, the header check. The user's script or CI job (the API client) sends a REST request with `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. API routes read only this header. If a request also carries a cookie, the Bearer token decides the user. If the header is missing, the scheme is not Bearer, the token is empty, or the token lacks the `pat_` prefix, the server returns 401 with a generic body. This happens before any hash or database read.

10. API call, the lookup. For a well-formed header, the server hashes the presented token with SHA-256. It finds the row by `token_hash` through the unique index. The row must exist, have no `revoked_at`, and have an `expires_at` in the future. There is no cache, so every call reads the row. An unknown, revoked or expired token gets the same 401 body as a malformed one. If the database check itself fails, the server returns 503 with a generic "retry later" body, and the token is not accepted. A CI script should retry a 503 after a wait and treat a 401 as final.

11. API call, success. If the row is valid, the request runs as the row's `user_id` with that user's full access. The document says no scopes are set. The server sends the normal API response.

12. Last-used update. After responding, if `last_used_at` is empty or more than an hour old, the server fires a background conditional update. It sets `last_used_at` to now only if the field is still empty or over an hour old. Two simultaneous calls can both send it, and the second matches no row. The write uses the server's own database connection. If it fails, is slow, or the server restarts first, the API response is unaffected and nothing retries it. A failure is logged without the token.

13. Revoke. The user clicks Revoke and confirms. The request goes to the server with the session cookie. If the token is not found or belongs to another user, the server returns 404, the same for both cases. Otherwise it sets `revoked_at` to now and keeps the row. It returns success and the token leaves the list. The next API call with that token gets 401. If the database write fails, an error is returned, the token stays active, and the user can retry.

14. Expiry. At 90 days the token simply stops passing the lookup check (401) and drops off the list. It cannot be renewed, so the user creates a new one. A name can be reused once the old token is revoked or expired.
gaps: The document does not say how the browser's create, list and revoke requests identify the server routes or HTTP methods. It also does not say how the revoke request names the token, such as by `id` or by name.
The document does not say what the existing signed-out refusal looks like (status code or redirect). It says this was not checked.
The document does not say how the server decides a request is an API route as opposed to a settings endpoint. It says the route wiring was not checked.
The document does not say what the database is told to do to 'check the name' beyond the uniqueness rule. It also does not say whether the name check is case-sensitive.
The exact 4xx status codes for a duplicate name and for the 10-token limit are open.
